nameStory: Goose Grass gets its name from the finger-like arrangement of its seed heads, which resembles the spread toes of a goose's webbed foot. The scientific name Eleusine comes from Eleusis, an ancient Greek city where similar grasses may have grown, while 'indica' means 'from India,' hinting at this world traveler's origins.
description: Goose Grass is a low-growing annual grass that forms dense, flattened mats close to the ground. This tough little grass typically grows 6-18 inches tall but spreads outward rather than upward, creating circular patches in lawns, sidewalk cracks, and compacted soil areas. Its most distinctive feature is the arrangement of 2-8 finger-like seed spikes that radiate from the top of each stem like spokes on a wheel.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: The unmistakable finger-like seed spikes radiate from a central point like a bird's foot, usually 3-6 spikes per stem that feel rough and papery when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms flat, dense mats that hug the ground in circular patches, staying low even when unmowed and feeling springy underfoot

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green blades that fold along the midrib, creating a distinctive boat-like crease you can feel with your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flattened and compressed at the base, spreading outward in a star pattern from the center of each clump

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, dark brown seeds arranged in neat rows along each finger spike, becoming loose and easily shaken off when ripe

habitat: Goose Grass thrives in disturbed, compacted soils where other plants struggle, making it common in sidewalk cracks, driveways, parking lots, and heavily trafficked lawn areas. You'll find it in full sun locations throughout New England's urban and suburban areas, particularly where foot traffic or vehicles have compressed the soil. It's especially abundant around playgrounds, pathways, and the edges of athletic fields.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate later than most weeds, typically appearing in late spring when soil warms up, starting as small tufts of folded leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants rapidly expand into characteristic flat mats and produce their distinctive finger-like seed heads from mid to late summer, even in mowed areas.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and scatter in early fall, turning the seed spikes brown and papery before the first frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown patches mark where plants grew the previous year, with seeds lying dormant in the soil until spring warmth triggers germination.

funFact: Goose Grass is so tough it can actually set seed even when mowed weekly at golf course height, making groundskeepers everywhere shake their fists at this nearly indestructible lawn invader that laughs in the face of lawn mowers.
confusionNotes: Goose Grass is most often confused with crabgrass, but the finger-like seed arrangement is the dead giveaway - crabgrass has more branched, delicate seed heads while goose grass looks like someone glued 3-6 thick fingers together at the stem tip. Remember: if it looks like a bird's foot, it's goose grass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an invasive weed in New England, goose grass seeds are actually edible and have been used as emergency food during famines in other parts of the world, though the yield is quite low and harvesting is tedious.
compareHints: Goose Grass is the only Eleusine species commonly found in New England, making it unique among our grasses for its distinctive finger-like seed head arrangement. While other grasses like crabgrass or barnyard grass may form similar mats, none have that characteristic spoke-wheel pattern of thick, finger-like seed spikes radiating from a single point.
